title: Digital analysis of literature

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Traditionally, scholars have studied literature by intensively looking at individual written texts or perhaps comparing a few such texts. However, today, with the use of advanced computer technology, some researchers are aggregating and analysing massive quantities of information including words from thousands of texts. Franco Moretti, founder of the Literary Lab at Stanford University in the USA, is one such researcher. He tackles literary problems by scientific means: hypothesis-testing, computational modelling and quantitative analysis. He advocates understanding literature not by studying individual texts, but by applying rigorous scientific methods to study an enormous number of texts collectively. Only in that way, Moretti argues, can you identify broad literary patterns and currents. A good example of this approach can be found in the work of a team of researchers at Dartmouth College in the USA, led by Professor Daniel Rockmore. The Dartmouth group set out to study the evolution of the literary styles of authors writing in English between the 16th and the 20th centuries, looking at literary trends across many works. The research used data from 7,733 digitised books written by 537 authors available from the Project Gutenberg library.

He advocates understanding literature not by studying individual texts, but by applying rigorous scientific methods to study an enormous number of texts collectively.
Only in that way, Moretti argues, can you identify broad literary patterns and currents.

A good example of this approach can be found in the work of a team of researchers at Dartmouth College in the USA, led by Professor Daniel Rockmore. The Dartmouth group set out to study the evolution of the literary styles of authors writing in English between the 16th and the 20th centuries, looking at literary trends across many works. The research used data from 7,733 digitised books written by 537 authors available from the Project Gutenberg library.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The Dartmouth researchers focused on the usage of ‘content-free’ words like prepositions (e.g. ‘of’, ‘in’, ‘to’), conjunctions (e.g. ‘and’, ‘but’), and articles (e.g. ‘the’, ‘a’, ‘an’) which, Professor Rockmore explained, are useful for stylistic analysis because they do not convey meaning. While content words can yield data about subject matter, content-free words can provide data for the analysis of literary style. Professor Rockmore says that content-free words form the ‘glue’ of language: they carry little or no meaning on their own but form the bridge between words that do convey meaning and thus provide useful stylistic fingerprints for literary characteristics.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The Dartmouth researchers found that the writing of authors in the 18th and 19th centuries was stylistically similar, and was strongly affected by the writing of their predecessors from previous centuries. Therefore 18th- and 19th-century authors displayed a remarkably similar choice of words, phrasing, meaning and grammar. This resulted in significant stylistic stability, with styles remaining relatively unchanged for extensive periods. However, authors writing in the 20th century were most affected by other 20th-century writers. In other words, the past seems to be exerting a diminishing stylistic influence on the present. If one believes that writing style is significantly related to popular speech, then the diminishing importance of the past might be traced to the speed with which spoken communication is changing today. According to Professor Rockmore, another reason for this may be that because of the huge number of new books now coming on the market each year, people devote less of their reading time to the ‘classics’ and are thus less affected by them.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The prize-winning American novelist Lionel Shriver agrees that her own writing style has not been very much affected by older literary works, and suggests that this is likely to apply to other modern writers as well. She confesses that while she devoured classics in her teens and 20s, she now reads contemporary fiction almost exclusively. With all the other things she does, like writing book reviews, she doesn’t often get around to the classics. She says, ‘I’ve discovered that I don’t have the patience any longer – for the long philosophical digressions, for example. I bet I’m not alone in this reduced tolerance for the stylistic traditions of the past.’

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: While digital literary analysis has been hailed by some scholars as an opportunity to revitalise the field of literary studies, others remain unconvinced. Dartmouth English professor Aden Evens fears that the new methods of analysis provided by digitisation will appeal to different people, including university administrators who to some extent control or at least help decide on the funding of academic research. Evens continues, ‘What I am worried about is that we are asked to set aside what most distinguishes the humanities – our ability to perform critiques of ambiguity – and instead we are being asked to supplant it with a view of knowledge that promotes certainty, statistical or numerical style analyses, absolute and clear distinctions.’

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Other scholars feel that quantitative methodologies will never replace the more usual ways of studying literary texts. In interpreting what the numbers mean, a literary scholar has to bring in all the knowledge of literature and authors that is applied in customary literary studies. Computer-based interpretation of texts, however, can provide opportunities to ask new questions about literature. According to James Hughes, a member of the Dartmouth team, researchers using computational tools do not claim to employ the ‘best’ approach to literature. ‘The point is really,’ writes Hughes, ‘that traditional analyses that take into account the intangible or unquantifiable factors can benefit from the addition of quantitative evidence.’
